text:
Recent evidence supports separating recommendation relevance from confidence in the judgment. A 2026 RecSys workshop paper finds that richer item metadata and longer histories improve LLM–human agreement, but item-level agreement remains moderate; judges are complementary diagnostic signals. NIST’s 2025 LARA similarly supports human-assisted assessment because LLM judgments can be biased and task-dependent. ([RecSys study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.23312), [LARA](https://www.nist.gov/publications/llm-assisted-relevance-assessments))

Practical protocol synthesized from these findings: show timestamped interaction histories plus candidate titles/descriptions, restricted to information available at recommendation time. Annotate four separate fields: choose-now relevance (supported/plausible/unsupported/unknown); redundancy (exact repeat, documented content overlap, none observed, unknown); explicit incompatibility (documented contradiction, none observed, unknown); and evidence sufficiency. Require supporting item IDs, history timestamps, or description excerpts. Similarity alone does not establish unwanted redundancy; interaction does not establish ownership, satisfaction, or current need. Missing compatibility evidence means unknown fit. Choose-now relevance remains a hypothesis unless the user directly confirms it.

Pilot the rubric with two independent annotators, revise ambiguous examples, then double-annotate a stratified subset across all four categories. Report per-field agreement, nominal or ordinal Krippendorff’s alpha as appropriate, unknown rates, and disagreement patterns; adjudicate while retaining original labels. If direct user feedback is available, ask what they would choose now and why, allowing “none” and “insufficient information.” Never infer mood, compatibility requirements, or simulator traits. Use annotations to explain failures while retaining the pinned macro validation HR@10 for selection. LLM consensus alone is insufficient validation: a 2025 study found stronger agreement among LLM assessors than with humans. ([SIGIR study](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/352747/))
